hero.caption:
Bishan Si (temple) on Wutai Shan.
Shown here is the temple's pailou, with a 4-character inscription and elaborate dougong.
The first temple, to occupy the spot where Bishan Temple is now located, was founded by Emperor Xiaowen (471-499 AD) of the Northern Wei dynasty. It was rebuilt as a Chan  (Zen) temple in 1486, and then in 1698 as Bishan Si under the sponsorship of Kangxi. The temple retains its Chan affiliation to the present day.

images.caption:
Ordination Hall. Bishan Si, on Wutai Shan
Bishan Si is the only temple on Wutai Shan with an ordination hall.  Inside the hall there is a set of arhats, and a Ming-dynasty ordination platform that displays a Burmese jade statue of the Buddha.

images.caption:
Buddhist lay people chanting the sutras. Bishan Si, on Wutai Shan
Although dressed like monks, this is a group of devotional Buddhist  lay people (including both men and women) who have come to the temple to chant the sutras.
The area under the eaves provides enough shade for the entire group to gather comfortably; this practical consideration is an obvious illustration, if one is needed, of why such eaves are a ubiquitous feature of Chinese architecture. Visitors (and especially photographers) to traditional Chinese temples and residential compounds will notice that the area under the eaves always seems to be in shadow, regardless of the time of day or the position of the sun.
